summary: Updates RFC 7450 (Automatic Multicast Tunneling) by changing relay discovery. It defines a DNS resource record, AMTRELAY, that publishes AMT relays for source-specific multicast channels in the reverse DNS zone of the sender's address.

eli5.summary: A phone book entry that tells you which helper to call to get a certain broadcast, found by looking up the sender's number.

questions: how are amt relays discovered with dns
subtitle: A DNS record, looked up by the multicast sender's address, that tells AMT gateways which relays can deliver that sender's traffic.

tldr.problem: An AMT gateway that wants a multicast stream from a source needs a relay that can receive traffic from that source, but there may be no multicast connectivity or pre-arranged peering between the sender's network and the receiver's.
tldr.mechanism: The sender publishes AMTRELAY resource records (type 260) in the reverse IP DNS zone of its address. The gateway looks up its source address there to find relay addresses or names, with rules for ordering, connecting and restarting discovery.
tldr.outcome: Gateways can discover relays for source-specific multicast channels without configured peering. The record is only a fallback after local discovery methods, and it needs a trusted DNS answer.

facts.label: DNS query rate limit
facts.value: no more than 10 per 100 ms by default

today: RFC 8777 is a Proposed Standard from April 2020 and updates RFC 7450. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why AMT Needs Relay Discovery
sections.content:
This RFC defines DNS Reverse IP AMT Discovery (DRIAD), a way for AMT gateways to discover AMT relays that can forward multicast traffic from a known source IP address. AMT (Automatic Multicast Tunneling, RFC 7450) carries multicast traffic over a unicast tunnel across network segments that cannot do multicast.

RFC 7450 already says relay selection should be more flexible than its own discovery method and may have to depend on the source of the traffic, because a relay can only forward what it is able to receive. It suggests DNS-based queries as one answer, and DRIAD is that answer. The goal is multicast connectivity between separate multicast-enabled networks without preconfigured peering, when neither the sending nor the receiving network is connected to a multicast-enabled backbone.

Once a tunnel is up, the relay receives native multicast and sends unicast tunnel-encapsulated traffic to the gateway. The gateway decapsulates it and forwards it as native multicast. The document updates RFC 7450 by extending its relay discovery procedure.
sections.eli5: Some networks cannot pass broadcasts along, so a helper wraps them up and mails them to a second helper who unwraps them. This RFC is about how the second helper finds the first.

sections.title: How the Lookup Works
sections.content:
The sender owns the AMTRELAY record and sets up its zone so that it lists the IP addresses or domain names of AMT relays, or of discovery brokers that advertise relays, which can receive its multicast traffic. The mechanism works only for source-specific multicast channels, written (S,G). The source address S is reversed and used as an index into the reverse mapping tree: in-addr.arpa for IPv4 or ip6.arpa for IPv6.

The worked example has five steps:

  • The end user's app joins the (S,G).
  • The join propagates through the receiver's multicast network until the AMT gateway gets a signal to join.
  • The gateway sends a DNS query for the AMTRELAY type at the reverse domain name of S, and the answer names the relay.
  • The gateway does the AMT handshake with the relay and forwards a membership report for the (S,G).
  • The relay propagates the join toward the sender and forwards the traffic through the tunnel, and the gateway delivers it as native multicast.

For an IPv4 source the only difference is the in-addr.arpa name. For the example (S,G) of (198.51.100.12, 232.252.0.2) the query name is 12.100.51.198.in-addr.arpa.. The address family of the tunnel is independent of the family of the multicast traffic.
sections.eli5: When you ask for a show, your helper looks up the sender's number in a special phone book and finds who can bring the show to you. That helper then sends the show in a tunnel.

sections.title: Choosing and Connecting to a Relay
sections.content:
The sender's record is a good way to find a relay that the sender knows, but not necessarily the best one for the gateway. A closer upstream relay would keep more of the path on native multicast. So a gateway should query the sender's record only when all of these hold: it must propagate a join over AMT because no RPF next hop can carry a native join, it is not already connected to a suitable relay, it has no configured discovery address that works, DNS-SD discovery using _amt._udp finds nothing usable, and the well-known anycast addresses from RFC 7450 find nothing usable.

Gateways SHOULD by default prefer relays in this order: DNS-SD, then the anycast addresses, then DRIAD. Administrative configuration MAY override it. Among DRIAD relays, the precedence from the record MUST be used ahead of the Destination Address Selection ordering of RFC 6724. Equal candidates SHOULD be chosen non-deterministically to support load balancing.

Gateways are RECOMMENDED to use a Happy Eyeballs algorithm (RFC 8305) to probe several relays at once and cut join latency. The RFC defines an AMT connection as established when the gateway receives, from a newly discovered relay, a valid Membership Query message that does not have the L flag set. The membership report is sent only to the chosen connection. A gateway MUST rate limit its DNS queries unless its DNS client already does, and by default SHOULD NOT allow more than 10 queries in any 100-millisecond period.

A gateway MAY connect to several relays and subscribe to the same traffic for active/active failover, but SHOULD NOT do so without guaranteeing adequate bandwidth.
sections.eli5: Before using the sender's phone book, your helper first asks nearby helpers, because a close one is better. Only if none can help does it look up the sender, and it may call several helpers at once and keep the first that answers.

sections.title: When to Restart Discovery
sections.content:
Restarting discovery is always safe, but if it picks a different relay the multicast tree upstream changes, which can drop or duplicate packets. Gateways should therefore avoid a full restart during routine cases, such as before each normal Request message in a membership update cycle. This section is guidance for operators and implementers. The RFC adds four events to the list from RFC 7450, including a new source address, a network change, heavy loss or congestion, and no traffic arriving after a join.

If no traffic arrives for any subscribed (S,G), restarting is appropriate. Repeated restarts SHOULD use a random exponential back-off with a RECOMMENDED initial_timeout of 4 seconds and a RECOMMENDED maximum_timeout of 120 seconds. A gateway restarting for this reason MUST put the relay on a hold-down that SHOULD last no less than 3 minutes and no more than 10 minutes.

The L flag in a Membership Query is the preferred way for a relay to say it is overloaded or shutting down. A gateway that sees it should generally restart discovery, and SHOULD avoid that relay for about 10 minutes. To avoid many gateways rediscovering at once after a transient network event, a random delay of at least 10 seconds by default is recommended. Discovery per tunnel is independent: restarting one pseudo-interface does not require restarting the others.
sections.eli5: If the show never arrives, your helper waits a bit, then tries another source, waiting a little longer each time. It also remembers not to call the helper that failed for a few minutes.

sections.title: The AMTRELAY Record
sections.content:
The AMTRELAY resource record has the mnemonic AMTRELAY and type code 260, and it is class independent. Its RData has an 8-bit precedence, a 1-bit D-bit (Discovery Optional), a 7-bit type and a variable-length relay field.

Precedence works like the PREFERENCE field of the MX record in RFC 1035: relays in records with a lower value are attempted first. If the D-bit is 0, the gateway MUST do AMT relay discovery and get a Relay Advertisement before sending a Request message. This suits load balancers or brokers that are not full relays. If the D-bit is 1, the gateway MAY send a Request directly. The D-bit MUST be 0 when the relay operator gave no information.

The type says what the relay field holds: 0 for empty (no AMT relay should be used for traffic from this source), 1 for a 4-octet IPv4 address, 2 for a 16-octet IPv6 address, and 3 for an uncompressed wire-encoded domain name. Records with an undefined type SHOULD NOT be considered. For type 3, the D-bit and precedence apply to all the A or AAAA records of that name.

In a zone file the record is written as precedence, D-bit, type and relay, all REQUIRED, and for type 0 the relay MUST be .. The example for source 198.51.100.12 lists an IPv4 relay and an IPv6 relay at precedence 10, plus the name amtrelays.example.com. at precedence 128 with the D-bit set. Servers that do not know the type can use the unknown-record format of RFC 3597.
sections.eli5: Each phone book entry says how important it is, whether you can call straight away or must ask first, and then gives either a number or a name to look up.

sections.title: DNS Zone Setup
sections.content:
A gateway usually knows only the source and group addresses, so the reverse IP tree is the best place to look. AMTRELAY records are therefore RECOMMENDED in reverse IP zones. They MAY also appear in other zones, for example to delegate from reverse zones as described in RFC 2317, but this document defines no meaning for records found any way other than a reverse IP lookup. Any CNAMEs or DNAMEs found during the lookup MUST be followed, which supports zone delegation.

If a gateway must wait for DNS, it follows ordinary DNS client practice. When it retries, it SHOULD use random exponential back-off, with a RECOMMENDED initial_timeout of 1 second and a RECOMMENDED maximum_timeout of 120 seconds.
sections.eli5: The sender must put its entry in the phone book that is sorted by number, because that is the only thing the gateway knows about the sender.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DRIAD makes AMT easier to use without a multicast backbone, so operators should read the security section of RFC 7450. AMT gives no integrity protection to multicast data packets. An off-path attacker who learns the gateway IP, relay IP and relay source port could inject data for a joined (S,G) by spoofing the relay. Operators are encouraged to protect received traffic, for example by opportunistic use of IPsec when IPSECKEY records are available.

The AMTRELAY answer should reach the client unmodified, and there must be a trust relationship between the client and the DNS server. That can be end-to-end DNSSEC validation, or a secure channel to a trusted server such as TSIG, SIG(0), DNS over TLS or DNS over HTTPS. A forged record could cause a denial of service or make receivers process traffic from a source under the attacker's control.

Multicast, especially between domains, also carries congestion risk. Operators are advised to monitor traffic, authenticate at ingest, rate limit and use circuit-breaker techniques as in RFC 8085.
sections.eli5: If someone puts a fake entry in the phone book, you could call the wrong helper. So the answer has to come over a trusted line, and the tunnel itself should be protected too.

messages.note: The join propagates with RPF until the gateway gets a signal to join.

messages.note: Asked for the reverse IP domain name of S.

messages.note: Gives the relay address, 2001:db8::c:f in the example.
